Chapter 2: Lessons from Tribal Societies and the Power of Mutual Dependence
If we're really trying to understand what's missing in modern life, maybe the best thing we can do is look at societies that have kept the old ways alive. Think about small, traditional groups—sometimes called tribes—where people truly rely on each other for survival. In those settings, every single person counts, and everyone’s needed. There just isn’t much space for the kind of isolation that, sadly, so many of us feel today.
Picture this: a group gathered around a fire, winding down after a long day. They’re sharing stories, passing food, and laughing together. Kids are running around, watched by more than just their parents. If someone’s sick, others will step up and help. If there’s danger, the whole group responds—no hesitation. In moments like these, lines between individuals start to blur, and the needs of the group come first. It’s a way of living that’s demanding, sure, but it can also be incredibly rewarding.
Anthropologists have noticed something pretty interesting: people in tribal societies often say they’re happier, and they tend to have fewer mental health issues than folks in more developed countries. That’s not because life is easier for them—it’s actually the opposite. Every day is a struggle for food, shelter, and safety. But here’s the thing—their deep sense of belonging and shared purpose acts like a shield against despair.
Here’s a story that really brings this to life. Back in the early days of European settlement in North America, some colonists were captured by Native American tribes. What’s fascinating is that, even when given the chance to go back, some chose to stay with the tribe. The tight bonds and clear sense of purpose in tribal life drew them in, even more than the comforts of the world they’d left behind. This baffled the settlers, who thought their own society was obviously better. But for those who’d lived on both sides, the choice was simple.
We see this same pattern show up in other situations, too. During war, or in the middle of a disaster, people often come together in tight-knit groups—almost like modern-day tribes. Suddenly, differences like class, race, or background matter less. What matters is being willing to help, and to accept help. And in those moments, that heavy sense of isolation so many of us carry? It just melts away.
Imagine a firefighter, completely wiped out after a tough night fighting flames, finding comfort in the understanding of their team. Or neighbors, thrown together by a flood, discovering a strength they never knew they had. These experiences change people—they shape how we see ourselves, and each other.
So, what’s the lesson here? It’s simple, but powerful: we’re at our best when we’re part of something bigger than ourselves. The bonds we form in tough times aren’t just a reaction to danger—they reveal what it really means to be human. And when life settles down, that craving for connection doesn’t just disappear.
Sure, modern society has its perks. But it often falls short of giving us the deep ties that make life truly meaningful. Our challenge, then, is to find ways to rebuild those connections—even in a world that’s obsessed with independence. Because it’s not enough to just be safe or comfortable. We need to feel needed. And we need to know, deep down, that we belong.
